hook.title: The Lazy Speaker's Secret Weapon
hook.content: Conjugating dozens of German verbs can feel intimidating. Modal auxiliary verbs are your shortcut: conjugate just ONE modal verb in Position 2, and the rest of your thought travels to the end as an uninflected, easy infinitive!

footnotes.title: Satzklammer Principle
footnotes.content: The sentence bracket (Satzklammer) frames your sentence between the conjugated auxiliary verb and the final bare infinitive.

pattern.title: The Modals: können, müssen, wollen
pattern.content: German 'ich will' = I want (not future 'I will'!). In ancient English and German, 'will' always meant desire or intent. English still uses this original meaning in living phrases like 'free will', 'will to live', 'against my will', and 'willingly' (related to Latin voluntas → voluntary). When you say 'Ich will lernen', you assert your will: 'I desire to learn'! Likewise, 'ich kann' = I can (originally 'to know', living in cunning, uncanny, and beyond my ken), and 'ich muss' = I must. Notice how 'ich will lernen' requires no extra 'zu' (to)!

footnotes.title: Free Will & Voluntary
footnotes.content: Old English 'willan' meant 'to desire/wish'. English shifted it into a future tense marker, but kept its true desire meaning in 'free will', 'will to live', 'last will and testament', and Latin-borrowed 'voluntary'.

pattern.linguist_note: Why do German modals drop the -t ending in 'er kann', 'er will', 'er muss'? English does the exact same thing! We say 'he can' (never 'he cans!'), 'he will' (never 'he wills!'), and 'he must' (never 'he musts!'). Both languages preserve this unique ancient pattern!

exercises.prompt: Which modal verb translates to 'I want' (as in 'free will' and 'will to live')?

vocab_hints.note: false friend: means 'want', as in 'free will', 'will to live', or 'voluntary'
direct twin of English 'shall' (Shakespeare: 'thou shalt' ↔ German 'du sollst')

exercises.explanation: German 'ich will' means 'I want/desire'. English keeps this original meaning in 'free will', 'will to live', 'against my will', and 'voluntary'.

exercises.prompt: Match the modal phrases to their English meanings:
exercises.target_answer: ich kann, ich muss, ich will, haben
exercises.meaning: I can, I must, I want, to have
exercises.explanation: Modal auxiliaries anchor German sentence frames and simplify communication.

exercises.prompt: Which English is built the German way?
exercises.explanation: The modal holds position 2 and the bare infinitive closes the bracket, so today lands between the two halves of the English verb pair. English used to allow this ('I know not where the shepherds keep'); German never left it.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: Verb first for a question, then the subject
The bare infinitive closes it: kommen
exercises.explanation: The verb flipped to the front for the question and the infinitive stayed parked at the end — Kann ich … kommen is one bracket, not two loosened words.
exercises.affirmation: You heard the flip and the parked infinitive — that is the bracket working in your ear.

exercises.idea: you're telling me your plans for visiting: you can come tomorrow
cues: Who can? → ich kann (can = know-how, as in 'beyond my ken')
When? → morgen, riding inside the bracket
The bare infinitive closes the bracket: kommen goes last

vocab_hints.note: English 'tomorrow' literally means 'to the morrow' (to the morning!)

idea_parts: what? → kommen, and the bare infinitive closes the bracket
exercises.explanation: The Satzklammer wraps around 'morgen', placing bare infinitive 'kommen' at the caboose.

diagnosis.slip: the modal's ending jumped onto the infinitive
diagnosis.cue: Only the modal conjugates — ich kann stays whole, and kommen stays bare. When two verbs share a sentence, the bracket decides who bends.

summary.outcome: Say what you want or can do by placing a bare infinitive at the end.
summary.takeaway: Use modal + bare infinitive at the end to assemble complex thoughts immediately.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the will ≠ will drills — separating ich will (free will) from the future, with sollen ↔ shall.

twist.prompt: Same thought, but tomorrow comes first: I want to learn German tomorrow. (Something still has to hold position 2.)
twist.explanation: Fronting fills position 1, so the verb keeps position 2 and the subject slips in behind it — the bracket never breaks, it just re-grips.

können.context_translation: I can come / I am able to come.
können.etymology_derivation: Originally meant "to know/understand". Preserved in English "can", "cunning" (knowing how), "uncanny", and "beyond my ken" (beyond my knowledge).

müssen.context_translation: I must / have to go now.
müssen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English "must" (root shifted to sibilant -ss-).

wollen.etymology_derivation: Retains original Germanic sense of desire/intent: "free will", "will to live", "against my will", and "willingly" (cf. Latin voluntary).

wolf.context_translation: The wolf lives in the forest.

eis.context_translation: I would like to eat an ice cream / ice.

europa.etymology_derivation: Inherited from Middle High German Eurōpā — the same Greek name both languages share. [wiktionary]

zahlen.context_translation: I would like to pay, please.
zahlen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *talōną 'to count' — cognate with English tale; German z is the shifted t. [wiktionary]

rindfleisch.context_phrase: Ich kaufe Rindfleisch für die Suppe.
rindfleisch.context_translation: I am buying beef for the soup.
rindfleisch.etymology_derivation: Rindfleisch — a compound of Rind (cow, from Proto-Germanic *hrinþaz, ultimately PIE *ḱerh₂- head) and Fleisch (flesh); English lost Rind and took French beef instead. [wiktionary]

gegen.context_phrase: Das Spiel beginnt gegen drei Uhr.
gegen.context_translation: The game starts at about three o'clock.
gegen.etymology_derivation: The twin of English against — both from Proto-Germanic *gagin; the entry lists against as a cognate. [wiktionary]

esszimmer.context_translation: The meal is in the dining room.
esszimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of essen and Zimmer; essen corresponds to English eat via the t to ss shift. [wiktionary]

hitze.context_phrase: In der Hitze trinken wir viel Wasser.
hitze.context_translation: In the heat we drink lots of water.
hitze.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *hitjǭ (heat); the page says cognate with Dutch hitte and related to English heat — the t-to-z shift shows between heat and Hitze. A cousin of the heiß-hot pair. [wiktionary]

zweig.context_phrase: Die Katze klettert auf den Zweig.
zweig.context_translation: The cat climbs onto the branch.
zweig.etymology_derivation: From Old High German zwīg, from Proto-Germanic *twīgą. English twig is the listed cognate, keeping the t where German shifted to z. [wiktionary]

haselnuss.context_phrase: Ich mag Schokolade mit ganzen Haselnüssen.
haselnuss.context_translation: I like chocolate with whole hazelnuts.
haselnuss.etymology_derivation: Hasel + Nuss, the exact calque of hazelnut; the page names English hazelnut as a cognate, and Nuss is the documented twin of nut with t shifting to ss. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
